hook.title: Your component runs once. Ever.
hook.lede: Delete `useMemo`. Delete `useCallback`. Delete every dependency array. A Pyreon component runs when it mounts, and a signal change updates the one DOM node that shows it, so there is nothing left to memoise.

before.label: React 19

after.label: Pyreon

sections.caption: Same counter, same derived value, same list. On the left, `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` exist only to tell React what not to redo. On the right, `add` is a plain function created once, `computed` tracks its own dependencies, and `<For>` keys rows with `by`. No dependency array anywhere, because a signal records who read it.

sections.title: Zero re-renders, by construction.
text: In React the counter body runs on every click. It builds a new element tree and the reconciler diffs it against the old one to find a single changed character. That is why `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `memo` and dependency arrays exist: every value in the body is recreated on each render, so you have to say which ones are stable.

In Pyreon the body runs once, at mount. A handler defined in the body is created once. A `computed()` is created once and tracks what it reads. When `count` changes, `count` notifies the text node bound to it, and nothing else in the tree is visited.
You lose the afternoon you used to spend on "why did this re-render?". There is no second render to ask about.

sections.title: Ten lines in, one binding out.
sections.text: This is what `transformJSX` from `@pyreon/compiler` emits for a counter. The static markup becomes a cached template string. The only dynamic part is one line: `_bindText(count, __t2)` subscribes that text node straight to the signal. Clicking `+` writes one text node, and that is the whole update.

sections.title: Watch it happen in your own app.

items.title: Open the reactive overlay
items.text: Press `Ctrl+Shift+R` in any dev build (or call `$p.reactivity()` in the console). It is built into `@pyreon/runtime-dom` and tree-shaken from production builds, so there is nothing to install.

items.title: Read the Health and Activity tabs
items.text: Health lists orphan signals, high fan-out and deep chains. Activity shows the latest updates with the chain of writes that caused each one.

items.title: Press Pick, then click a value
items.text: In the Inspect tab, press Pick (or call `$p.pick()`) and click text bound to a single signal or computed. The panel shows that signal and its change chain. Text built from several signals shows nothing, by design: the link is recorded exactly when the binding is made, never guessed.

sections.title: Live or static, decided before you run anything.
sections.text: The Reactivity Lens prints the compiler's own verdict next to every JSX expression in your editor, served by `pyreon-lint --lsp`.

items.title: `live`
items.text: Reads a signal in a tracked position. It updates.

items.title: `live·prop`
items.text: A reactive component prop, wired as a getter on `props`.

items.title: `live·attr`
items.text: An attribute that re-evaluates when its signals change.

items.title: `static`
items.text: Evaluated once. If you expected `live`, you just found the bug.

items.title: `hoisted`
items.text: A provably static subtree lifted to module scope.

sections.text: Signal reads inside reactive scopes re-evaluate when the signal changes. Signal reads outside reactive scopes evaluate once and become static.

sections.title: The rules, straight.
sections.text: Run-once has a small set of rules. They are what the compiler emits, and the lint rules and the Lens catch the common slips.

items.title: Destructuring props captures once
items.text: `const { name } = props` copies the value at setup, so the text never changes. Read `props.name`, or use `splitProps(props, ['name'])`, whose pieces keep their getters.

items.title: A `const` derived from props stays live
items.text: `const name = props.name ?? 'stranger'` is inlined at its JSX use site and re-reads `props.name`. A `let` is never inlined.

items.title: An early return runs once
items.text: `if (loading()) return <Skeleton />` pins the component to whichever branch was true at mount. Use `<Show when={loading} fallback={…}>`, or return an accessor.

items.title: Write with `.set()`, not a call
items.text: `count(5)` is a read that ignores its argument. `count.set(5)` and `count.update(fn)` write.

items.title: Prefer plain JavaScript? Opt in to Plain Mode
items.text: Plain Mode is an opt-in compile-time dialect: `'use plain'` at the top of a file (or `pyreon({ plain: true })` app-wide) lets you write `let count = state(0); count++`. Destructured props stay live and early returns on a reactive condition become reactive. It compiles to the same signal code.

sections.text: We publish where we lose, so you can trust where we win: in the same record Solid mounts a deep 2,047-component tree 1.15–1.18× faster, creating a signal is about 5× slower than in Preact Signals, and the same keyed-table app is 17.2 KB gzip against Solid's 7.5 KB.

items.a: Same run-once model, and we are happy to say so. The compiler does more of the wiring: a bare signal read binds the signal itself with no closure, signal reads in component props become getters, and a `const` derived from props is inlined so it stays reactive.

Yes. React identifies hooks by call order across renders. Pyreon has no second render, so a hook is an ordinary call made during setup. What you cannot do is call one after setup: inside a click handler, a `setTimeout` or after an `await`.

`<For each={items} by={(i) => i.id}>`. The key prop is `by`, because JSX reserves `key`. Each row's bindings are separate, so toggling one todo touches one attribute on one `<li>`, and reordering moves existing nodes by key.

items.q: How do I know a value is live?
items.a: Look at the Lens hint in your editor. It is the compiler's own `live` or `static` verdict for that expression, so it shows what the build will do. `pyreon check` catches the common slips, such as destructured props, before you commit.
